speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Despite elevated uncertainty, the economy is in a solid position.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low, and the labor market is at or near maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has come down a great deal but has been running somewhat above our 2 percent longer-run objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We believe that the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Following growth of 2.5 percent last year, GDP was reported to have edged down in the first quarter, reflecting swings in net exports that were driven by businesses bringing in imports ahead of potential tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This unusual swing has complicated GDP measurement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Private domestic final purchases, or PDFP, as we call them—which excludes net exports, inventory investment, and government spending—grew at a solid 2.5 percent rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Within PDFP, growth of consumer spending moderated, while investment in equipment and intangibles rebounded from weakness in the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Surveys of households and businesses, however, report a decline in sentiment over recent months and elevated uncertainty about the economic outlook, largely reflecting trade policy concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It remains to be seen how these developments might affect future spending and investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, the median participant projects GDP to rise 1.4 percent this year and 1.6 percent next year—somewhat slower than projected in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions have remained solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 135,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, remains low and has stayed in a narrow range for the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wage growth has continued to moderate while still outpacing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance and consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection for the unemployment rate in the SEP is 4.5 percent at the end of this year and next, a bit higher than projected in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.3 percent over the 12 months ending in May and that—excluding the volatile food and energy categories—core PCE prices rose 2.6 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have moved up over recent months, as reflected in both market- and survey-based measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Respondents to surveys of consumers, businesses, and professional forecasters point to tariffs as the driving factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation this year is—is 3 percent, somewhat higher than projected in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median inflation projection falls to 2.4 percent in 2026 and 2.1 percent in 2027.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent and to continue reducing the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to determine the appropriate stance of monetary policy based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Changes to trade, immigration, fiscal, and regulatory policies continue to evolve, and their effects on the economy remain uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The effects of tariffs will depend, among other things, on their ultimate level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Expectations of that level, and thus of the related economic effects, reached a peak in April and have since declined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Even so, increases in tariffs this year are likely to push up prices and weigh on economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The effects on inflation could be short lived—reflecting a one-time shift in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also possible that the inflationary effects could instead be more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Avoiding that outcome will depend on the size of the tariff effects, on how long it takes for them to pass through fully into prices, and, ultimately, on keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our obligation is to keep longer-term inflation expectations well anchored and to prevent a one-time increase in the price level from becoming an ongoing inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we act to meet that obligation, we will balance our maximum-employment and price-stability mandates, keeping in mind that, without price stability, we cannot achieve the long periods of strong labor market conditions that benefit all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may find ourselves in the challenging scenario in which our dual-mandate goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that were to occur, we would consider how far the economy is from each goal and the potentially different time horizons over which those respective gaps would be anticipated to close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For the time being, we are well positioned to wait to learn more about the likely course of the economy before considering any adjustments to our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection projects—participant—median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.9 percent at the end of this year, the same as projected in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection declines to 3.6 percent at the end of next year and to 3.4 percent at the end of 2027, a little higher than the March projection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These individual forecasts are always subject to uncertainty, and, as I have noted, uncertainty is unusually elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, these projections are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, the Committee continued its discussions as part of our five-year review of our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We focused on issues related to assessing the risks and uncertainties that are relevant for monetary policy and the potential implications for policy strategy and communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our review includes outreach and public events involving a wide range of parties, including Fed Listens events around the country and a research conference that we held last month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are open to new ideas and critical feedback, and we will take on board lessons of the last five years in determining our findings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We intend to wrap up any modifications to our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After that, we will consider enhancements to our suite of communications tools, including the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve had three months of, of favorable inflation readings since the high readings of January and February, and that’s, of course, highly welcome news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Part of that just is that services, core services—both housing services and nonhousing services have really been grinding down toward levels that are—that are consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the good news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve had goods inflation just moving up a bit, and, of course, we expect—as you—as you point out, we, we do expect to see more of that over the course of the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It takes some time for tariffs to work their way through the chain of distribution to the end consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good example of that would be, goods being sold at retailers today may have been imported several months ago—before tariffs were imposed—so we’re beginning to see some effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do expect to see more of them over coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do—we do also see price increases in some of the relevant categories like personal computers and audio-visual equipment—things like that that are attributable to tariff increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, we look at surveys of businesses, and there, there are many of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you, you do see a range of things, but, but many, many companies do expect to—to, to put all or—some or all of the effect of tariffs through to the next, next person in the—in the chain and, ultimately, to the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today—you know, the amount of these—the, the amount of the tariff effects, the size of the tariff effects, their duration, and the time it will take are all highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that is why we think the appropriate thing to do is to hold where we are as we learn more, and we think our policy stance is, is in a good place—where we’re well positioned to react to incoming developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you look at the forecast, you will see that people do generally expect inflation to move up and then to come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we can’t just assume that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we don’t know that, and, you know, our, our job is to make sure—one of our jobs—to make sure that a one-time increase in inflation doesn’t turn into an inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that, again—that will depend on the size of the effects, how long it takes for them to come in, and, and, ultimately, on, on keeping inflation expectations anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would focus most on the—on the nearer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you think—as you get out to the—to the later years, it’s hard to—it’s hard for anybody to know where the economy is going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You didn’t see people moving their longer-term, you know, estimate of the neutral rate, for example, at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and those things are probably slow moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And by the way, it was—it was a similar move from the December SEP to the March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see the, the effects of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we learned in April, after the March meeting, that substantially higher tariffs were likely, and then since then, the estimates of where the tariffs will be have actually moved back down, although still at an elevated level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re adapting in real time, and what you see is, you know, an, an accumulation of individual assessments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we said was that uncertainty has, has—uncertainty about the economic outlook has diminished but remains elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many, many surveys say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and, and, that’s—that’s actually a line from the Tealbook, which you can see in five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember to check that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] HOWARD SCHNEIDER.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe the world will be over by then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No—but if you think of that, tariff uncertainty—uncertainty really peaked in April and since then has come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that’s really what that’s just acknowledging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s diminished but still elevated—that it’s uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that’s an accurate statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do—we do, of course, monitor all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think if you look at the overall picture, you know, what you’re seeing is 4.2 percent unemployment and an economy that’s growing at a—at a rate hard to know, given the, the unusual flows in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it appears to be 1½, 2 percent—maybe a little better than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sentiment has come up off of its very low levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still—it’s still depressed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, you can—you can point to things—the housing market is a longer-run problem and also a short-run problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think it’s indicative of—you know, basically, the situation is, we have a longer-run shortage of housing, and we also have high rates right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the best thing we can do for the housing market is to restore price stability in a sustainable way and, and create a strong labor market, and that’s the best thing we can do for the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You asked about the job market—again, look at labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look at wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look at job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re all at healthy levels now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I would say you can see perhaps a very, very slow continued cooling, but nothing that’s troubling at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we watch it—we watch it very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, again, the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to economic developments, and—for now—and we’ll be watching the data carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is very much the conversation we had today and yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There, there are many, many different scenarios—many combinations of scenarios where inflation does or doesn’t prove out to be at the levels we think and where the labor market does or doesn’t soften.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think what, what you see people doing is looking ahead at a time of very high uncertainty and writing down what they think the most likely case is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one holds these, these rate paths with a great deal of conviction, and everyone would agree that they’re all going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that—you can make a case for, for any of the rate paths, I think, that you see in, in the SEP. And, you know, we do this once a quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—it’s a hard thing to do at this—particularly at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it does reflect—you know, if you see somebody writing down, you know, a, a rate path that involves cuts, that’s them saying, “Yes, I think we will get to a place, more likely than not, where cuts will be appropriate.” And it could be—it could be a joint probability of a number of possible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, remember how much uncertainty we face, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—it’s—again, it’s very, very hard to say when that will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that the time will come; it come—could come quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It could not come quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As long as the economy is solid, though—as long as we’re seeing the kind of labor market that we have and reasonably decent growth and inflation moving down, we feel like the right thing to do is to be where we are, with where our policy stance is, and just learn more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in particular, we feel like we’re going to learn a great deal more over the summer on tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do—we hadn’t expected them to show up much by now, and they haven’t, and we will see whether—the extent to which they do over, over coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that’s going to inform our thinking, for one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, we’ll see how the labor market progresses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, at some point, it will become clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t tell you exactly when that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, meanwhile, we’ll be watching, watching the labor market very carefully for signs of weakness and strength and tariffs for signs of, of what’s going to happen there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, there are many developments ahead, you know, even in the near term—developments are expected on tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we, we don’t yet know with any confidence where they will settle out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have an estimate, and it’s a pretty—I think all estimates are now pretty close together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s—it’s, yeah, highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people are managing to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, the, the pass-through of tariffs to consumer price inflation is a whole process that’s very uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, as you know, there are many parties in that chain: There’s the manufacturer, the exporter, the importer, the retailer, and the consumer, and each one of those is going to be trying not to be the one to, to pay for the tariff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But together, they will all pay for it together—or maybe one party will pay it all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that process is very hard to predict, and we haven’t been through a situation like this, and I think we have to be humble about our ability to forecast it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s why we need to see some actual data to have—to make better decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we’d like to get some, some more data, and, and, again, in the meantime, we can do that because the economy remains in solid condition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right, we—and, as is often the case, we have a pretty healthy diversity of views on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We did have strong support for today’s decision and broad agreement that our policy stance does leave us in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would point to two factors, and you mentioned them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The first is just that parties have a diversity of forecasts, and, and they do align with, with where—with where their dots are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you have a higher inflation forecast, you’re going to be less likely to be writing down, you know, more, more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But as—remember, as we see more data, we’re going to learn more about where inflation is headed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means when it is time to look at, at normal—at sort of, at, you know—resuming our normalization process, the differences you may—you see should be smaller because we’ll have seen actual data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right now, it’s just a forecast in a very foggy time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the first part—is forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Secondly, people can look at the same data, and they can evaluate the risks differently, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that includes, you know, the, the risk of higher inflation, the risk it’ll be more persistent, the risk that the labor market will weaken—people are going to have different assessments of that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you put that in there, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are the two ways that, that—the two things, I think, that drive these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember, though, with—as I mentioned earlier—with uncertainty as elevated as it is, no one holds these rate paths with a lot of conviction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s really where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a function of those things, and I think as the data come in, you should see those differences diminish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you just look backward at the data, that, that’s what you would say, but that’s not—we have to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the thing that every forecaster—every outside forecaster and the Fed is saying is that we expect a meaningful amount of inflation to arrive in coming months, and we have to take that into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think a backward-looking look would, would lead you to a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we, we can’t—we have to—we have to look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And because the economy is still solid, we can take the time to actually see what’s going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It, it’s, you know, the—there’s a range of possibilities on how, how large the, the inflation effects and the other effects are going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll make smarter and better decisions if we just wait a couple of months or however long it takes to get a sense of, of really what, what is going to be the pass-through of inflation and what’re—what’s going to be the effects on spending and on hiring and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, from my standpoint, it’s—it’s not complicated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What everyone on the FOMC wants is a good, solid American economy with a strong labor market and, and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think our policy is well positioned to—right now to, to deliver that and, and to be able to respond in a timely way as the data lead us around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy’s been resilient, and part of that is our stance, and, again, we think we’re—we’re in a good place on that to respond to significant economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is what matters to us—pretty much, that’s all that matters to us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m—I’m not thinking about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m thinking about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, you know—I, I wouldn’t want to speculate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What—one way to get at that from an economic standpoint—we, of course, don’t comment on immigration policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not ours to make or comment on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what you see is a—an, an unemployment rate that has been really solid and at a low level—not really increasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been in a—in a good range and well within the range of mainstream estimates of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means, like, part of that is that labor demand and labor supply are kind of moving down at the same rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Labor demand is, is softening—you see that in job creation—but it’s still kind of at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And labor supply is, is diminishing because the, the immigration numbers that we see are, are much lower than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the—those two factors, supply and demand—that’s what has kept the, the unemployment rate in a reasonably, you know, stable place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The first track is our—is our policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that is reflected in the consensus statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we, we’ve said that we would finish that and announce it by the end of the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re well along in that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve had the meetings that we need to have, and we’re now going to be going into [cough]—pardon me—into discussions about, you know, specific changes to language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—that’s the framework part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re going to do in the meetings this fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Actually, what we did at this meeting, though, is we, we sort of prepared the ground for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had a—we had a meeting where we talked at a high level about a number of ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The SEP is part of it—you know, other—many, many other ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are a number of ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People offered a really—it was a great conversation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Number of ideas—but we’re—we’re going to look at those with staff briefing and a lot of thought in the fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say, when it comes to changing communications, you know, I would only do—I would only support things really that only—implement things that have very broad support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, you want to be really careful, because I think our communications are pretty well received.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not broken, so more is not necessarily better—but better is better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re going to be looking at ways to do—to do things that will improve the clarity of what we do for the benefit of, of the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, the, the forecast for inflation in December was 2½ core PCE for 2025—the forecast was 2½ percent—which is a good inflation forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think what we’ve learned is that—and this was long before we had any idea of what the actual policies would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve learned the tariffs are going to be substantially larger than, than forecasters generally thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we, we don’t—our, our forecasts are generally not particularly different from those of other, you know, well-resourced forecasting operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we learned—and particularly in April—was that substantially larger tariffs were coming and that that would mean higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you—now you see—you saw 2½ percent forecast in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw 2.8 percent in March, and you see 3.1 percent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s six-tenths higher inflation for 2025, and that’s—that’s a big part of, of the change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that’s due to the effects of, of the tariffs that are—you know, we, we don’t know where they’re going to land, but it’s pretty apparent they’re going to land higher than outside forecasters were really guessing at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I mean, we’re trying to restore price—the best thing we can do for the—for the public that we serve is restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we can, and we will, restore price stability, meaning 2 percent inflation on a durable, sustainable basis—that and also maximum employment—and if we, we restore those things, that’s the best thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The best thing we can do for the American people—for, for households and businesses—that is the ultimate thing that we can deliver.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they can make their decisions without having to think about inflation all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in the meantime, we have to keep rates high to keep—to get inflation all the way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not very high—let’s be honest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say policy is modestly or moderately—probably modestly now—restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at the economy, it’s not performing as though it were performing under very strict monetary policy—very restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say probably modestly restrictive—and so what it will take is, is confidence that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, I would say, without tariffs, that confidence would be building because if you—if you see what’s happening with nonhousing services and housing services, which are the other two big pieces other than goods, those are coming down really nicely now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we have to learn a little more about, about tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know—I don’t know what the right way for us to react will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s hard to know with, with any confidence how we should react until we see, really, the size of the effects—then we can start to make a better judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we’re doing, and I think we can—we can take the time to do that, because unemployment is 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Real wages are moving up at a—at a healthy clip now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And inflation is, you know—2.3 percent headline inflation over a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a good economy, and a solid economy with decent growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not—I’m not saying that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, from our standpoint, what I can say is that the, the U.S. economy is in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains at 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, real wages are moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a—it’s a good—job creation is at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Unemployment, again, as I said, low—labor force participation at a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we’re waiting for to reduce rates is, is to understand what will happen with, with, really, the tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there’s a lot of uncertainty about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Every forecaster you can name who, you know—who is a professional, you know, forecaster with, with adequate resources and forecasts for a living is forecasting, you know, a pretty significant—everyone that I know is forecasting a meaningful increase in inflation in coming months from tariffs because someone has to pay for the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it will be someone in that chain that I mentioned: Between the manufacturer, the exporter, the importer, the retailer— ultimately, somebody putting it into a, a good of some kind or just the consumer buying it—and, you know, all through that, that chain, people will be trying not to be the ones who, who pick up the cost.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, the cost of the tariff has to be paid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some of it will fall on the end consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that because that’s what businesses say—that’s what the, the data say from past—so we know that’s coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we just want to see, see a little bit of that before we make judgments prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I mean, you’re—monetary policy has to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is elementary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to be looking—I always—we always talk about the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s always forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if you know—at the very beginning of the pandemic, you know, we cut rates to zero immediately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing had happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we took very aggressive forward looking—because we knew things were going to be unusually difficult.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, this, this is something we, we sort of know is coming—we just don’t know the size of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, the economy seems to be in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the labor market’s not crying out for a rate cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Businesses, you know, were in a bit of shock after April 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you see business sentiment—you talk to business people now—there’s a very different feeling now that people are working their way through this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they, they understand how they’re going to go, and it’s—it, it feels much more positive and constructive than it did three months ago, let’s say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, again, we think that our current stance of monetary policy is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see them at all as, as in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] So—but we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We work hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say this—so we are careful stewards of public resources, and sometimes you need to show that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to do a buyout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to—going to show the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to demonstrate that we are good stewards of public resources.” So we thought—and I, I thought—that this is a time when we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve—we grow about—our headcount has grown at about 1 percent a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So over the course of a couple of years, we’re going to—we’re doing a careful scrub of the Board and all of the Reserve Banks, and we’re going to find 10 percent of employees who can do something else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Where, where we can—we can streamline our operations—and we, we think we can get there in a year, in a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we can do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think the—we think the, the—this is, this is without taking risk to carrying out our critical missions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is something you do very carefully—thoughtfully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you do it, again, respecting that we have critical missions to carry out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve had experience—a lot of experience—in my prior careers, you know, with headcount reductions and things like that, and this is how you do it professionally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You do it carefully—thoughtfully—with a lot of planning, and you do it over a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I think it’s—I think the Fed will be fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think no one will notice any decline in our ability to carry out our missions, and I think it’s just us wanting to demonstrate to the public that we are actually good stewards of their—of their resources.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—we’re effectively wiping out 10 years of headcount growth with this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I mean, we just—we wanted to show that, you know—that we’re good stewards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re just at the very beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, we’re doing a buyout program.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to—we’re going to hit that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think many organizations find that they can—that they can do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t want to do it every year or anything, but you can do it at intervals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you, you wind up not, you know—not interfering with your ability to perform your jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so, you know, we don’t—we don’t sit around and debate or really discuss—we, we take fiscal policy as fully exogenous.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we, we actually, you know, really didn’t talk about, about the bill or the contents of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still evolving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, when, when it gets close—closer—remember also we have a very, very large economy, and that the effects will be at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I, I expect that they’ll—they may already be in—but they will be in by the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll make an estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s not a major thing; it’s nothing that we discuss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It, it may have been mentioned a couple of times—but as something that’s coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think the outcome is—you know, we don’t know the outcome yet there—so, hard to be real specific.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, two things—one, the data we get right now—we, we can do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not concerned that we can’t do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not the—that’s not the point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The point, really, is that we are starting to see, you know, layoffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and important gatherers of data are saying that they’re—they’re having to cut back on the size of their surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s going to lead to more volatility in the surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we should take a step back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, from our standpoint—and I think the standpoint of businesses and governments and everyone—having really good data on the state of the economy at any given time is a huge public good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It helps.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t just help the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It helps the government, it helps Congress, it helps the executive branch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: More importantly, really, it helps businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They need to know what’s going on in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The United States has been a leader for many, many years in this whole project of measuring and understanding what’s happening in, in our very large and dynamic economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I hate to see—I hate to see us cutting back on that because it, it is a real benefit to the general public that people in all kinds of jobs have the best possible understanding of what’s happening in the economy and, and, hence, what’s likely to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hard to measure what’s going on in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If, if you read—there was a book called—well, it’s really remarkable how many things you need to understand to estimate U.S. GDP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very, very difficult—and it’s so important that we get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just would—I just would say it’s not a place to—I would want to keep investing in that, you know, for the good of the general public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the framework goes back to—the framework document goes back to 2012, and it’s—it’s the Committee’s document.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not like we’re going to invent a brand new way to do things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—it’s been an evolving document, so it shouldn’t depend on who the Chair is at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It should depend on what’s happening in the economy and what the Committee wants to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yeah, it isn’t really tied to any particular Chair, and, you know, we used to renew it every year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we do it every five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but I, I don’t think anybody—I’ve never heard anyone raise this issue that, you know, a new Chair might want to come in and go in a completely different direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I really—I really don’t think that’s right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, that’s not—not going to be up to me to decide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, we’re watching—like everybody else is—what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I really don’t have any comment on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, possible that, that we’ll see higher energy prices—what’s tended to happen is, when there’s turmoil in the Middle East, you may see a spike in energy prices—but tends to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those things don’t generally tend to have lasting effects on inflation, although, of course, in the 1970s, they famously did, because you had a series of very, very large shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we haven’t seen anything like that—that—like that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy is far less dependent on foreign oil than it was back in the 1970s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, but— MATT EGAN.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A quick follow-up—I’ve just got to ask you about artificial intelligence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some technology executives have recently been warning that AI could wipe out a large chunk of entry-level jobs and significantly increase the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m wondering how concerned you are, if at all, about the threat that AI poses to employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is the question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I wouldn’t—I, I—we all see those announcements, including one today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t overread a, a couple of data points, because, you know, AI should be creating jobs at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be replacing—it may be doing both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Anyone who’s done any work with it—with AI—will, will have been a little bit stunned at how capable it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s just a different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think this is something that certainly has transformational potential—and probably we’re in the very early stages of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They say what you’re seeing now compared to what you’ll see in two years is, is going to be very different and even more effective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s really hard to know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, of course, there are optimists who feel like it’s going to make everybody much more, you know—much more productive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there are those who think it’s going to replace an awful lot of jobs right across the income spectrum—you know, white collar, blue collar, and everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t—we don’t have a “house view” on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But this is—this is going to be a very important question for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—it’s certainly a time of real change—you know, from a geopolitical standpoint, from a trade standpoint, from an immigration standpoint—you see this not just here, but everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s—there’s quite a lot going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t change the way we do monetary policy in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, but—and it doesn’t change our objectives or what we need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, these, these things are not really our issues—they’re really issues for elected governments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All of those issues are really for elected governments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there’s no question it’s a time of, of real, real change—and very hard to see where that goes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Will it be—there have been many, many things written about how it’s going to be a more inflationary time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s possible; it’s not guaranteed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, AI could cut in a very other direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: AI could make people much more productive and—and push in the other direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really what we’re about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t, you don’t see—you don’t really see unemployment going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t see increased slack, really—I mean, at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember, you’re at 4.2 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that was for many, many years—that was an extremely low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It happens to have come up off of an even lower level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we came out of the pandemic, we were as low as 3.4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But 4.2 percent is probably at the low end of estimates of the longer-run, you know, sustainable level of natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t—I guess I wouldn’t agree with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, in terms of wages—you know, real wages after inflation have been moving up sort of more than was consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re still moving up at a—at a healthy clip—and I think much more consistent with 2 percent inflation, given, given a, a reasonable assessment of, of trend productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a pretty good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you’re right that the level of job creation has come down, but so has the supply of workers—the change in the supply—the, the new supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve seen—you’ve seen the unemployment rate remain pretty stable at 4.2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been as high as 4.3, but, you know, those are—those are good numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a pretty good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s—the thing is, there’s—a more concerning thing is, there’s not—there are not a lot of layoffs, but there are not a lot of, of job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The number—if you’re out of work, it’s—it’s hard to find a job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But very few people are being laid off at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—an equilibrium we watch very, very carefully, because if there were to be, you know, significant layoffs and the job-finding rate were to remain this low, you would have a lot—you would have an increase in unemployment fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that hasn’t happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It really hasn’t happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—so the U.S. economy has defied all kinds of forecasts for it to, to weaken, really, over the last three years, and it’s been remarkable to see—just again and again when people think it’s going to weaken out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Eventually it will, but we don’t see signs of that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there are a number of people on the Committee who wrote down no cuts this year but some cuts next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re not saying there’s zero possibility of other things, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, it’s—think of it as the least unlikely path in a situation like this where uncertainty is very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think—again, people write—they write down their, their rate paths, and they do not have, like, a really high conviction that this is exactly what’s going to happen over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one feels that way about their rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not easy to, to be—to do that with confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would just say it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t rule things in or out—certainly, a hike is not the base case at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something people are writing down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in the meantime, we do the best we can with these forecasts, and I, I think they’re—they’re representative of, you know, of the different forecasts and different reaction functions that people on the Committee have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So thank you very much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks.
